planting.note: Detach individual rounded stem segments in spring, let the cut callus for several days, then set atop dry gritty mix to root; wear gloves, since the sap is a skin and eye irritant.

directions: This is the true globosa that the more sprawling, mat-forming Euphorbia pseudoglobosa is so often confused with in cultivation, distinguished by a dense mound of tightly packed, spineless, more or less spherical stem segments arising from a swollen woody base rather than trailing loosely across the soil surface. Leaves are minimal and quickly shed, so nearly all ornamental interest comes from the neat, marble-like stacking of the stem segments themselves. It occurs naturally only on a handful of stony coastal hills between Port Elizabeth and Uitenhage in South Africa's Eastern Cape, where it is now classified as endangered due to habitat loss, making nursery-propagated stock the only responsible source. Grow in full sun in an extremely fast-draining mineral mix, water sparingly, and keep the crown dry through winter to prevent rot at the base of the clustered segments.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Break off short branch sections, let the cut end callus a few days, then root in gritty succulent mix; a pendent habit suits a hanging container best.

directions: One of the two wild parent taxa behind the popular hybrid 'Baby's Necklace', this Eastern Cape subspecies grows as a cliff-dwelling succulent on sheer, exposed sandstone faces along the Kouga River, where its slender, pendent stems hang free of soil entirely. Fused pairs of thick, fleshy, gray-green to bluish leaves stack into four-angled columns along each branch, the margins often flushing purplish-red under strong light and drought stress, distinguishing it from the flatter, more triangular leaf pairs of the plain species form. Small cream to pale-yellow tubular flowers cluster at the branch tips in late summer and early fall. Because it evolved rooted in shallow rock crevices rather than open ground, it is best grown in a shallow pan or hanging pot in bright, filtered light with a very fast-draining gritty mix, watering only once thoroughly dry.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online
